sweep_summary: Karitiâna (kari1311) is not in the catalog. All 13 title-keyword items attached to it in Glottolog are noise: the Glottolog reference pages (checked for 629194, 653101, 596760, 579970) show 'Karitiâna [ktn] (computerized assignment from "perceptual"/"gestural")', and the items are English/German/French/Spanish/clinical prosody papers with no bearing on Karitiâna; none downloaded, priority none. First-hand statements were read from three open sources already held by the project from the earlier reading (Storto 1999 MIT dissertation pp.45-49, 79; Storto & Demolin 'Pitch Accent in Karitiana' USP preprint p.4-5; Everett 2006 Rice dissertation pp.107-110 via scanned) and three newly downloaded items (Landin 1983 SIL dictionary, pronunciation key silent on placement; Rocha/Silva 2011 USP thesis, silent; Storto & Demolin 2002 BLS 28, silent). All three primary sources agree: stress is predictable, on the final (rightmost) syllable of the stem, overridden by a long-vowel syllable (rightmost heavy wins; codas never heavy); CVi.CViC disyllables with initial stress are analysed as epenthetic; some suffixes are inherently stressed and primary stress goes to the rightmost stressed unit; H/L tone is assigned from stress (Storto's 'pitch accent'), while Everett argues the accent is cued mainly by loudness. Recommended coding: fixed final with quantity-sensitive (long-vowel) override, 'last heavy, else last'. Not obtained: Storto & Demolin 2017 book Karitiana Phonetics and Phonology (ARSOM; HAL record has no file; priority high), Landin & Landin c.1973 SIL phonology (sil.org blocked; medium), Rodrigues 1999 CUP survey (second-hand quote only; low), Storto & Demolin 2012 De Gruyter survey chapter (paywalled; low).org, Crossref and HAL API lookups.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: primary stress on the final (rightmost underlying) syllable of the root/stem. Long-vowel nuclei are heavy and always attract stress, so a non-final long vowel takes stress away from a light final syllable; with several long vowels the rightmost long vowel bears primary stress. Codas do not count for weight. Inherently stressed (class I) suffixes such as nominalizer -pa take primary stress (root keeps secondary); class II suffixes and all prefixes are never stressed; in any word with several stressed units (incl. compounds) primary stress is on the rightmost one. Disyllabic CVi.CViC roots with identical vowels surface with initial stress, analysed as stress assigned before epenthesis of the final vowel. Tone (H* plus boundary L%/H%) is assigned from stress ('pitch accent system').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Storto 1999:83-86 and Storto & Demolin sec.2.2: in root + stressed-suffix words (e.g. kookoto'pa 'bridge', o.ky.'pa 'weapon') primary stress on the suffix and secondary stress on the root's stressed syllable; all roots of a compound are stressed with primary on the rightmost. Everett 2006:108 adds rhythmic secondary stress on every other syllable preceding the final primary (e.g. first syllable of a trisyllable), 'often on the same order of magnitude (in loudness) as that of the primary stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Heavy (long-vowel) nuclei override finality (sa:ra 'alligator', 'de:so 'mountain', 'pa:si 'squash'); (ii) disyllabic CVi.CViC roots with two identical short vowels have initial stress ('pi.kip 'bark', '?i.rip 'tapir', kir<i>k 'mosquito') -- Storto: final vowel epenthetic; not in longer words (ki.ri.'rit 'frog') nor when the final nucleus is long (pi.'pi:t); some same-shape words are regular (ka.'rak, do.'kon); (iii) Everett 2006:110 lists residual lexical exceptions pa.'?i.ra 'wild/angry', 'ojim; (iv) unstressed class II suffixes (-na adjectivizer, imperative -a) and prefixes fall outside the stress domain, so surface stress can be non-final in the word ('e.dna 'pregnant', a.'ta.ra 'go!').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/stem plus inherently stressed suffixes, not the whole grammatical word: prefixes and class II suffixes are extrametrical, so 'final' means final in the stem. Statements based on citation forms and words in isolation (Storto & Demolin F0 figures of isolated words; disyllables in isolation always HL tonally regardless of stress). Storto 1999 ch.2 sec.2.2 also describes phrasal stress deletion/L-insertion under stress clash. Everett 2006 sec.7.1 disputes the 'pitch accent' characterization on acoustic grounds (accent = loudness/spectral tilt; pitch mostly intonational) but agrees on placement.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe the single Karitiana speech community (Arikém branch of Tupian, approx. 350 speakers in Rondônia per Storto & Demolin), glottocode kari1311; no dialect differentiation reported. Note the terminological split: Storto (1999) and Storto & Demolin call it a predictable 'pitch accent system' (tone assigned from stress), whereas Everett (2006) argues it is plain stress accent realized by loudness/spectral tilt; placement facts agree across sources.

new_statements.reading: Karitiâna word stress is predictable and right-edge oriented with quantity sensitivity restricted to vowel length: stress falls on the final (rightmost) syllable of the stem unless the stem contains a long-vowel syllable, in which case the rightmost long-vowel syllable is stressed (Storto & Demolin p.4 make the 'rightmost heavy, else final' rule explicit; saara 'alligator' initial vs so'oot 'to see' final vs pyypyyp 'owl' final). Closed syllables do not count as heavy. Apparent initial-stress CVi.CViC disyllables (pikip, ?irip, kirik) are treated as underlying monosyllables whose final vowel is epenthetic and stress-invisible. Some suffixes (e.g. nominalizer -pa) are inherently stressed, prefixes never; in derived words and compounds primary stress goes to the rightmost stressed unit, other stressed roots keeping secondary stress. Everett 2006 independently confirms default final stress with alternating secondary stress and heavy-nucleus attraction from acoustic data, notes a few lexical exceptions (pa.'?i.ra, 'ojim), and argues the accent is cued by loudness more than pitch. Tone (H/L) is assigned from stress, which Storto calls a pitch accent system. on the catalog's classification: fixed final stress with weight-sensitive (long-vowel) override, i.e. an unbounded right-oriented 'last heavy, else last' system.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Storto-based account (final/rightmost-heavy stress with a small class of initially stressed roots) and adds the same stress-clash-avoidance mechanism Storto 1999 (pp.77, 82-86) describes: -ka- and r-/ry- are inserted between a prefix and a verb root whose first syllable is stressed. Gives no placement rule of its own, so it neither confirms nor challenges 'rightmost heavy, else final'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given; this is a syntax paper. It presupposes that stress is a property of individual verb roots (some carry a lexical feature [+Init stress]), that the affirmative prefixes na-/ta- take the extended forms naka-/taka- before such roots, that r-/ry- insertion after the polar-response prefix keeps two stressed syllables from being adjacent, and that the stressed syllable of a monosyllabic verb root (a pyt'y 'Eat!') is its final one.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated as such; the [+Init stress] feature on some verb roots (e.g. tak- 'pound', põn- 'hunt' take naka-/taka-, oky- 'kill', oty- 'bathe' take na-/ta-) implies stress is not uniformly root-final

tone_statements.translation: According to Storto (1999), in Karitiana 'tones are assigned on the same metrical plane on which stress is computed'. In other words, the author states that the tones are predictable from the stress patterns of the words of an utterance. Specifically, she recognises the existence of an H* pitch accent ... [fn.1] Storto (1999) and Storto & Demolin (2005) call the Karitiana system pitch accent. However, it must not be confused with others also called pitch accent such as that of Japanese, in which words are marked as (un)accented in the lexicon

sources.quote: Word accent in Karitiana is, in the absence of intervening factors, placed on the final syllable in the word. This was the basic conclusion reached by Storto (1999:79) and alluded to in Landin (1984). [p.107] ... sources.quote: The assignment of stress in Karitiana is predictable based on phonological and lexical information. The stressed syllable in a root is always the rightmost, unless a heavy syllable is present (that is, a syllable with a long vowel), in which case, it will bear stress, as in (2). In case a root has more than one heavy syllable, as in (4), the rightmost heavy syllable is stressed [p.4] ... In case more than one stressed lexical item is present in a word, primary stress is assigned to the rightmost stressed unit without exception. [p.5]
sources.note: Restates Storto 1999 with acoustic (F0) data from three speakers: root stress rightmost, unless a long-vowel syllable is present, then the rightmost heavy syllable; initial-stress disyllables (kyr<y>k 'gnat') explained by final-vowel epenthesis; stressed suffixes; primary stress on the rightmost stressed unit in derived words/compounds; tone (H/L) assigned from stress. Confirms Storto 1999.

sources.quote: Karitiana seems to be an interesting language to compare with Japanese in terms of rhythm because both languages have a number of prosodic characteristics in common: • The same number of syllable types (4: CVC, CV, VC and V) • Contrastive vowel length • Pitch accent (unpredictable in Japanese; predictable in Karitiana, as described in Storto & Demolin 2005) [...] It is possible that Karitiana and Japanese pattern similarly with respect to ∆C because both languages have pitch accent (Storto 1999, Storto & Demolin 2005) and this kind of metrical phenomena plays a role in mora-timed rhythm.
